bibliographic.title: Evaluating ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4.0 Responses on Hyperlipidemia for Patient Education
bibliographic.authors: Thomas J. Lee, Abhinav K. Rao, Daniel J. Campbell, Navid Radfar, Manik Dayal, Ayham Khrais
bibliographic.citation_apa: Lee, T. J., Rao, A. K., Campbell, D. J., Radfar, N., Dayal, M., & Khrais, A. (2024). Evaluating ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4.0 responses on hyperlipidemia for patient education. Cureus. https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.61067

methodology.study_design: comparison of ChatGPT-3.5 versus ChatGPT-4.0 across three prompt forms using Cleveland Clinic hyperlipidemia FAQs
methodology.sample_description: 25 frequently asked questions on hyperlipidemia from the Cleveland Clinic, prompted in three forms (no prompting, patient-friendly prompting, physician-level prompting)
methodology.sample_size: 25 questions per prompting condition across two ChatGPT versions
methodology.technology_context: ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4.0 for patient education on hyperlipidemia

eligibility.exclusion_reason: The study empirically compares ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4.0 accuracy, comprehensibility, and response length for hyperlipidemia patient education in healthcare, but the provided text contains no discussion of conversational governance, accountability, human oversight, compliance controls, guardrails, observability, audit, or related operational governance mechanisms.
eligibility.decision_rationale: Although the article uses specific LLMs in a regulated healthcare education context, its objective and findings concern output accuracy and readability rather than governance of conversational AI systems. No governance, oversight, risk control, or accountability frameworks are described in the available text.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Absence of governance-related constructs is clear from title, abstract, methods, results, and discussion in the provided excerpts.

appraisal.notes: Methods are clearly described for comparing two ChatGPT versions across three prompt forms using a fixed FAQ set. Ethics, reflexivity, and detailed limitations are not evident in the provided text. Findings are reported with categorical scoring and statistical tests, but generalizability is limited to one clinical topic and one FAQ source.

cerqual.explanation: The study is internally coherent for evaluating ChatGPT response quality in healthcare patient education, but methodological scope is narrow and the provided text offers no evidence relevant to conversational governance in regulated LLM systems.

coding.theme: LLM response quality for medical patient education
coding.subtheme: version and prompt sensitivity in healthcare FAQs

synthesis.main_claim: ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4.0 provide largely accurate hyperlipidemia patient-education responses, with no significant accuracy difference between versions, while ChatGPT-4.0 produces more concise and readable output and better adapts to different prompt styles.
synthesis.contribution: Offers empirical comparison of free versus paid ChatGPT versions for healthcare FAQ-style patient education using a structured prompting protocol and accuracy categorization.
synthesis.limitations: Provided text does not detail study limitations; future research on diverse question formulations and handling of incorrect information is noted.
synthesis.use_in_review: Not suitable as central or supporting evidence for conversational governance in regulated LLM systems; at most marginal contextual background on LLM use in healthcare patient education.

evidence.claim: Study focuses on ChatGPT output quality, not governance
evidence.excerpt: This study compares the accuracy, comprehensibility, and response length of the free and paid versions of ChatGPT for patient education on hyperlipidemia.

evidence.claim: Specific LLMs and empirical comparison design
evidence.excerpt: ChatGPT versions 3.5 and 4.0 were prompted in three different ways and 25 questions from the Cleveland Clinic's frequently asked questions (FAQs) on hyperlipidemia.

evidence.claim: Responses scored for correctness and readability metrics
evidence.excerpt: Responses were categorized as incorrect, partially correct, or correct. Additionally, the grade level and word count from each response were recorded for analysis.

evidence.claim: No significant accuracy difference between ChatGPT versions
evidence.excerpt: Correct answers did not significantly differ between ChatGPT version 3.5 and ChatGPT version 4.0 (p = 0.586).
ChatGPT version 3.5 had a significantly higher grade reading level than version 4.0 (p = 0.0002).

evidence.claim: Healthcare regulated context with patient education application
evidence.excerpt: Healthcare providers can recommend ChatGPT as a source of patient education, regardless of the version used.

evidence.claim: ChatGPT described as AI chatbot, not governance system
evidence.excerpt: ChatGPT (OpenAI, San Francisco, CA, USA), an artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot created by OpenAI in November 2022, rapidly garnered widespread attention.

evidence.claim: No governance, oversight, or compliance mechanisms discussed
evidence.excerpt: Future research should explore diverse question formulations and ChatGPT's handling of incorrect information.
